newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine clarifies T-bill tax rules.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine clarifies T-bill tax rules.

text.p: Ukraine's explanation of complex tax rules on its high-return Treasury bills have made bankers optimistic Western investment in the market will rise.
The long list of regulations, issued this week for both local and foreign investors, clarifies when transactions on the primary and secondary markets will be taxed.

"The clarification will definitely improve things," said Serhy Monokha, chief of securities at the Donetsk-registered First Ukrainian International Bank, a Ukrainian-American-Dutch joint venture. "Foreign activity on the market will grow."
Many foreign buyers were reluctant to buy T-bills as they did not know how much tax they would pay.

"Until now, the discount Treasury-bill market was totally unclear, and it was not possible to do good business," said Kyrylo Shevchenko of the Finance and Credit Bank. "Now it's more or less clear, and that will be better."

Bankers said a 30-percent capital gains tax, a tax that particularly worried investors, would probably rarely apply since the regulations give banks significant leeway for making deductions to write off profits.
The rules, which apply immediately to all previous and future transactions, show how to calculate profits and losses and set a tax on purchases of T-bills at about 0.2 percent.
Foreign buyers will continue to pay a 15-percent tax on repatriation of profits, but Monokha said this would not discourage buyers.
"That charge was, is, and will be. It must be paid. When we suggest our service to investors and mention the 15 percent, it doesn't stop them," he said.

Yields on recent issues of T-bills, whose maturities run for three, six, nine and 12 months, have fallen to 50-60 percent from highs of more than 100 percent since Ukraine opened its T-bill market 18 months ago.
Last week, the central bank said foreigners could buy T-bills directly through Ukrainian banks, instead of allowing only the banks to buy, hold and sell bills for them.
But central bank officials previously said their share of the market would be limited to 35 percent.
